'''''Cotinus coggygria''''', [[synonym (taxonomy)|syn.]] ''Rhus cotinus'', the '''European smoketree''',<ref>{{PLANTS|id=COCO10|taxon=European smoketree|accessdate=17 January 2016}}</ref> '''Eurasian smoketree''', '''smoke tree''', '''smoke bush''', '''Venetian sumach''', or '''dyer's sumach''', is a Eurasian [[species]] of [[flowering plant]] in the [[Family (taxonomy)|family]] Anacardiaceae.

==Description==
It is a multiple-branching [[deciduous]] shrub growing to {{convert|5|-|7|m|0|abbr=off}} tall with an open, spreading, irregular habit, only rarely forming a small tree. The [[leaves]] are {{convert|3–8|cm|abbr=off|frac=4}} long rounded ovals, green with a waxy glaucous sheen. The autumn colour can be strikingly varied, from peach and yellow to scarlet. The flowers are numerous, produced in large [[inflorescence]]s {{convert|15|-|30|cm|abbr=on|frac=2}} long; each flower {{convert|5–10|mm|frac=8}} in diameter, with five pale yellow petals. Most of the flowers in each inflorescence abort, elongating into yellowish-pink to pinkish-purple feathery plumes (when viewed en masse these have a wispy 'smoke-like' appearance, hence the common name "smoke tree") which surround the small ({{convert|2–3|mm|frac=16|abbr=on|disp=or}}) [[drupaceous]] fruit that develop.

==Fossil record==
[[Macrofossil]]s of ''C. coggygria'' from the early [[Pliocene]] epoch have been found in Western [[Georgia (country)|Georgia]] in the [[Caucasus]] region.<ref>The History of the Flora and Vegetation of Georgia by Irina Shatilova, Nino Mchedlishvili, Luara Rukhadze, Eliso Kvavadze, [[Georgian National Museum]] Institute of [[Paleobiology]], [[Tbilisi]] 2011, {{ISBN|978-9941-9105-3-1}}</ref>

==Distribution and habitat==
The species is [[native species|native]] to a large area from southern Europe, east across central Asia and the Himalayas to northern China.

== Uses ==

=== Ornamental plant ===

It is commonly grown as an [[ornamental plant]], with several [[cultivar]]s available. Many of these have been selected for purple foliage and flowers.

The following cultivars have gained the [[Royal Horticultural Society]]'s [[Award of Garden Merit]]:-
*'Flame'<ref>{{cite web |url=https://www.rhs.org.uk/Plants/97510/Cotinus-Flame/Details |title="Cotinus" 'Flame' |publisher=RHS |accessdate=5 May 2020}}</ref> 
*{{tdes|'''Golden Spirit'''}}='Ancot'<ref>{{cite web |url=https://www.rhs.org.uk/Plants/137770/Cotinus-coggygria-Golden-Spirit-Ancot-(PBR)/Details |title="Cotinus coggygria" Golden Spirit='Ancot' |publisher=RHS |accessdate=5 May 2020}}</ref>  
*'Royal Purple'<ref>{{cite web |url=https://www.rhs.org.uk/Plants/97746/Cotinus-coggygria-Royal-Purple/Details
|title="Cotinus coggygria" 'Royal Purple' |publisher=RHS |accessdate=5 May 2020}}</ref> 
*'Young Lady'<ref>{{cite web |url=https://www.rhs.org.uk/Plants/147186/Cotinus-coggygria-Young-Lady-(PBR)/Details
|title="Cotinus coggygria" 'Young Lady' |publisher=RHS |accessdate=5 May 2020}}</ref> 

=== Dyestuff ===

The wood was formerly used to make the yellow dye called '''young fustic''' ([[fisetin]]),<ref>{{Cite EB1911 |wstitle=Fustic |volume=11 |page=375}}</ref> now replaced by synthetic dyes.<ref>{{cite web |url=https://www.britannica.com/technology/young-fustic |title=Young fustic |publisher=Encyclopaedia Britannica |website=Britannica.com |accessdate=5 May 2020}}</ref>

The species, along with other members of the sumac family, has been used to make red dyes for textiles including weft-wrapped [[soumak]] rugs and bags in the Middle East. The names ''sumac'' and ''soumak'' likely derive from the Arabic and [[Syriac language|Syriac]] word {{lang|syc|ܣܘܡܩܐ 'summāq'}}, meaning "red".<ref>Etymology of Sumac at [https://www.etymonline.com/index.php?search=sumac Etymonline.com] and also at {{cite web |title=Dictionary English Etymology – Origins – A Short Etymological Dictionary of Modern English Routledge 1958, Parridge) |url=https://www.scribd.com/doc/14047074/Dictionary-English-Etymology-Origins-A-Short-Etymological-Dictionary-of-Modern-English-Rouledge-1958-Parridge |url-status=dead |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20141012185830/http://www.scribd.com/doc/14047074/Dictionary-English-Etymology-Origins-A-Short-Etymological-Dictionary-of-Modern-English-Rouledge-1958-Parridge |archive-date=2014-10-12 |access-date=2017-09-15}} and [https://archive.org/details/etymologicaldict00weekuoft/]. Etymology of Rhus at {{cite book |last=Quattrocchi |first=Umberto |url=https://books.google.com/books?id=zIOvJSJs-IkC |title=CRC World Dictionary of Plant Names: Common Names, Scientific Names, Eponyms, Synonyms, and Etymology |publisher=Taylor & Francis US |year=2000 |isbn=978-0-8493-2678-3 |volume=IV R-Z |page=2306}}</ref>
